name: Carla Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying dental hygiene and therapy, so my week is anatomy, a lot of practice in the skills lab with mannequin heads, and some clinic shadowing on Fridays. I rent a room in a shared house with my cousin Rina, and I waitress at an Italian restaurant four nights a week. I pray every morning and go to church on Sundays. I use AI every day, for revision plans, flashcards and sorting my shifts, and I want to open my own clinic one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful assistant but not a revolution. It helps me revise and plan, and that's about all. People will always need someone to clean their teeth and tell them off about flossing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm fine about the job and a bit stretched on money. The loan doesn't cover rent, and tips are unpredictable. If things stay the same, I'd be okay but not comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the waitressing, keep using AI for revision and look for a paid dental assistant job on weekends. I'd save my tips in a jar and apply for every small grant. I'd also keep going to church, because it grounds me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, but tight. I'm optimistic by nature, and I know my money is the weak spot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you want your own clinic. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bright little clinic with two chairs, a friendly receptionist and my name on the door. I'd hire hygienists I trained myself. Dentists make more money, but hygienists see the same patients over and over, and that's where the trust comes from.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do the restaurant nights fit with your studies?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Busy and tiring. I'm on my feet from five till eleven, and on Fridays I'm in clinic at eight. I do flashcards on the bus. Tips on a good Saturday pay for a whole week of groceries.

say: I'd say it's a useful **assistant** but not a revolution.
I'd say people will always need someone to clean their **teeth**.
think: Privately, I'm fine about the job but **stretched** on money; the loan does not cover rent.
do: Keep **waitressing**, keep using AI for revision and look for a paid dental assistant job.
Apply for every small **grant** and save tips in a jar.
feel: **Good**, but tight; optimistic, with money as the weak spot.
S0.quote: Tips on a good Saturday pay for a whole week of groceries.
fieldNote: She is **optimistic** and already a daily AI user; money is the one clear pressure.
Her dream is a small two-chair **clinic** built on trust.

steps.text: Keep waitressing four nights a week at the restaurant
Look for a weekend dental assistant job
Apply for every small grant and bursary
Use AI for revision plans and flashcards

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say software will take over the booking, the notes, the imaging checks and some patient reminders. The hands-on cleaning and the chat stay with us. I'd say learn the tools and stand out from the people who don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I see it as a chance. If AI handles the admin, a hygienist can see more patients and earn more. But the big dental chains might cut staff, so I'd want to be independent one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the practice software during my placements, and use AI to build patient handouts. I'd keep waitressing for now. And I'd start looking at what it takes to run a small practice: insurance, rent and equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, with a small worry. It feels like the start of a long climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which parts of a dental hygienist's work do you think software takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin Rina, who does accounting, to go and learn the new tools right now. Bookkeeping is the kind of thing that goes first. She'd say I'm exaggerating, and I'd say I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your cousin Rina?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big chains, because they'd use software to cut hours. I'd want to avoid ending up in one that treats hygienists like machines. That's why I'd want to run my own place.

say: I'd say software takes **booking** and notes, while the hands-on cleaning and chat stay with us.
I'd say learn the **tools** and stand out.
think: Privately, I see a **chance**: with less admin a hygienist can see more patients and earn more.
Big dental **chains** might cut staff, so I want to be independent.
do: Learn the practice **software** in placements and use AI to build patient handouts.
Look into what running a small **practice** takes: insurance, rent and equipment.
feel: **Excited**, with a small worry; the start of a long climb.
S1.quote: I'd tell my cousin Rina, who does accounting, to go and learn the new tools right now.
fieldNote: She sees **opportunity** and moves early, but fears big chains cutting hours.
Her answer connects the change to her plan to own a **practice**, and she warns her cousin early.

steps.text: Learn the practice software during placements
Make patient handouts with AI tools
Research the costs of running a small practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a lot and we should face it with faith and work. I'd say there's still something only a person can do, like looking after a frightened patient. I'd say governments shouldn't let it move so fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the first one that really shakes me. Two years is nothing, and I wouldn't even have qualified. The thinking parts of dentistry, like diagnosis and scheduling, would be done by AI, and robots for hands-on work would be a few years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use every AI tool I can find to learn faster and finish my degree on time. I'd save everything from the restaurant, and ask my church community if anyone needs help with childcare or tutoring for pay. I'd also look into starting a small business with Rina, maybe a dental appointment service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I pray on it. I'd say I feel more alert than frozen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first month after hearing it was two years away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rina we should pool our savings and think about moving back with her parents if needed. We'd do it together. My mum would say come home, and I'd say I'm fine, and I'd probably be lying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your cousin and your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cost of getting it wrong. I'm the first of my family in university, and I've got a loan. If this goes bad, it's not just my future.

say: I'd say we should face it with **faith** and work, and governments shouldn't let it move so fast.
I'd say a person can still look after a frightened **patient**.
think: Privately, it **shakes** me: two years is nothing, and I wouldn't have qualified.
Diagnosis and scheduling would go to AI, and **robots** would follow a few years behind.
do: Use every AI **tool** to finish my degree on time and save everything from the restaurant.
Ask my church about paid **childcare** or tutoring, and plan a small business with Rina.
feel: **Anxious**, but I pray on it; more alert than frozen.
S2.quote: I'm the first of my family in university, and I've got a loan. If this goes bad, it's not just my future.
fieldNote: She meets the shock with **action** and faith, and uses community as a safety net.
The weight of being **first** at university raises the stakes beyond her own life.

steps.text: Use AI tools to finish the degree on time
Save every restaurant wage into one account
Ask the church about paid tutoring or childcare
Plan a small appointment-service business with Rina

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you start now. I'd tell friends to learn the tools, save money and not depend on one employer. I'd say that's what responsibility looks like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine. I'd graduate in three years, work as a hygienist for two, and use that time to build savings and experience. I'd be ahead of most people because I'm using the tools already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, take a job at a good practice, and start saving for my own equipment. I'd build a small side business, like a patient-reminder service for dentists. I'd also keep going to church, which keeps me calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful. Ready, even. It feels like a race I've trained for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years is a bit slower. What would you do with the extra time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to have a lease signed on a small clinic, or at least a plan with numbers. I'd have two chairs, a loan from the bank and a lot of nerves. And a good name, which matters in a small town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have built in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a big chain moves in before I do. They have money, and I'd have a loan. I'd want to have patients who trust me before a big chain arrives.

say: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if you **start** now.
I'd tell friends to learn the tools, save money and not depend on one **employer**.
think: Privately, I'd be **fine**: I would graduate, work as a hygienist for two years and build savings.
I'd be ahead of most people because I use the **tools**.
do: Finish the degree, take a job at a good **practice** and start saving for my own equipment.
Build a small **side** business such as a patient-reminder service for dentists.
feel: **Hopeful**, even ready; a race I've trained for.
S3.quote: I'd want to have patients who trust me before a big chain arrives.
fieldNote: Five years suit her **adaptive** style; she plans savings, a side business and a lease.
Her worry is **competition** from chains with more money, so trust with patients is her answer.

steps.text: Take a hygienist job at a good local practice
Start a patient-reminder service for dentists
Save toward my own clinic equipment

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a blessing and we should use it well. I'd say people should learn to work with the new tools and not be afraid of them. And I'd say community and family matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel good. I'd qualify, work a few years, and open my own practice within five. By 2036 I'd have my own patients and a few staff. The robots would arrive as helpers, not threats.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd study, work, save and keep learning the tools. I'd open a small clinic, hire a couple of hygienists, and use AI to run the books. I'd keep helping Rina with her business, and keep my faith.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm. A bit excited, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, how does your plan change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want a place with a play corner for kids and a plant by the window. I'd greet every patient by name. That's how you win over people who've had bad experiences in the dentist's chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people who don't use the tools get left behind. I'd like to help them, maybe by teaching a class at church. Ten years is enough for most people if someone shows them how.

say: I'd say ten years is a **blessing** and people should not be afraid of the new tools.
I'd say **community** and family matter more than ever.
think: Privately, I'd feel **good**: qualify, work a few years and open my own practice within five.
Robots would arrive as **helpers**, not threats.
do: Study, work, save and **keep** learning the tools.
Open a small **clinic**, hire two hygienists and use AI to run the books.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough for most people if someone shows them how.
fieldNote: The long runway lets her plan a **clinic** and she sees herself helping others.
Her faith and community give her **calm** that money alone does not.

steps.text: Qualify and work a few years as a hygienist
Open my own small dental clinic
Run a church class teaching people to use AI tools

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened? And is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one worries me most. I'd be unqualified, with a loan, and everyone watching me to succeed. What would help is a safety net for students and some honest warning from the government. One thing you didn't ask: I'm not afraid of change. I'm afraid of change that happens to people while everybody pretends it isn't happening.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of change. I'm afraid of change that happens to people while everybody pretends it isn't happening.
portrait: Carla is a **dental hygiene** student who rents a room with her cousin Rina and waitresses four nights a week.
She uses AI every day, prays each morning and wants to open her own **clinic** one day.
Traditional, free-market and adaptive, she moves early and builds **side** income and community ties.
Her fear is the two-year case, where she would be **unqualified** with a loan and her family watching.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case worries her most: unqualified, with a loan, and her family relying on her.
whatWouldHelp: A **safety net** for students and honest warning from the government.
